concept.name: Hedge ratio
concept.definition: The ratio of the size of the position taken in a hedging instrument (e.g., futures contracts) to the size of the exposure being hedged; it determines how much of the price risk is offset by the hedge.
concept.intuition: It is the proportionality dial on a hedge: ratio 1.0 means you hedge dollar-for-dollar; 0.6 means you take a hedge position only 60% as large as your exposure.
concept.mechanics: When the asset underlying the futures contract is the same as the asset being hedged, a hedge ratio of 1.0 is commonly used; when cross hedging, the hedger chooses the ratio that minimizes the variance of the hedged position. The number of contracts is N = h * Q_A / Q_F, where Q_A is the exposure size and Q_F the contract size.
concept.formula: h = (size of hedge position) / (size of exposure); number of contracts N = h * Q_A / Q_F.
concept.failure_modes: A naive 1.0 hedge ratio ignores differences in volatility and correlation between the exposure and the hedging instrument, so it can over- or under-hedge; it also assumes the spot-futures relationship stays stable over the hedge life.
concept.misconceptions: A hedge ratio of 1.0 is not automatically 'full protection': it is optimal only when spot and futures price changes move one-for-one, which cross hedges and basis risk routinely violate.
concept.example: A producer expecting to sell 2 million gallons of fuel hedges with 42,000-gallon futures contracts; at a hedge ratio of 1.0 this requires about 48 contracts, but at the optimal ratio of 0.8 it requires 38.

citations.source: John C. Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (8th ed.), Chapter 3 lecture slides: Hedging Strategies Using Futures
citations.section: Cross Hedging - Hedge Ratio; Optimal Number of Contracts
